title: Mosaic: Runtime-Efficient Multi-Agent Embodied Planning
one_liner: Mosaic makes a team of embodied agents act faster by keeping a shared world record in each agent's local frame and assigning actions with a constraint solver.
lead: A team of embodied agents has to keep track of what each agent can see, what each agent can reach, and which actions can happen at the same time. Most failures come from two sources: the agents lose track of the world after moving, or two agents choose actions that clash. Mosaic fixes both problems by storing objects in each agent's own coordinate frame and by choosing each step with a solver that enforces physical and coordination rules.

paras: In embodied planning, each agent sees only part of the scene. After moving, it must update where objects are, where teammates are, and which jobs are still open. If that record drifts, an agent may walk to the wrong place or try to pick up an object that is not there.

Coordination adds a second problem. Two agents may both go after the same object, block each other in a narrow space, or choose an order that cannot work in the real scene. Each failed action costs time because the system has to ask again, replan again, and execute again. Mosaic targets those wasted steps directly.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Keep each agent's world record in its own local coordinates, transform those records into a shared view, then choose the next joint action set with a solver so that the team only attempts compatible moves.

panels.title: 1. Two agents see different slices of the room
panels.viz_args: Agent A sees the table. Agent B sees the cabinet. No single view is complete.
panels.caption: Each agent starts with a partial view, so the team must combine local records.

panels.title: 2. Plain replay drifts after movement
panels.caption: If an agent moves and the world record is not transformed with it, later actions target stale positions.

panels.title: 3. Mosaic stores objects relative to each agent
panels.viz_args: Cup is 1 meter ahead of A. Door is 2 meters left of B.
panels.caption: Local coordinates stay simple to update because each record moves with the agent.

panels.title: 4. A solver picks a compatible joint step
panels.viz_args: A opens cabinet; B waits, then picks item after door is open.
panels.caption: The solver rules out clashes and keeps only action sets that can happen together.

panels.title: 5. Fewer failures means shorter runs
panels.caption: The team finishes sooner because it spends less time on repeated planning and failed actions.

steps.b: Record objects in each agent's local frame
steps.text: Each agent stores where objects are relative to itself, which keeps updates simple after motion because the record moves with the agent.

steps.b: Transform local records into a shared team view
steps.text: When agents need to coordinate, the system converts those local records into one shared scene description so each agent can reason about the same object.

steps.b: List candidate actions for every agent
steps.text: At each planning step, each agent proposes actions such as move, open, pick, or wait.

steps.b: Solve for a feasible joint action set
steps.text: A constraint solver chooses one action per agent while enforcing reachability, ordering, and collision-style rules so that the chosen set can really happen.
After the step runs, each agent refreshes its local record and the next planning round starts from a cleaner state.

paras: The paper changes two internal objects: the team memory and the step-level action selector. Instead of a loose text record of the world, it keeps a geometric scene record anchored to each agent. Instead of letting agents choose actions independently, it solves one joint decision problem at every step.
object.object: Team world record and joint action choice

hidden.name: State consistency across agents
paras: State consistency asks whether all agents are acting on a scene record that still matches the real world. This quantity is hidden because you only notice it after a failure: an agent reaches for empty space, repeats a job, or blocks a teammate.

Mosaic keeps consistency higher by storing positions relative to the observing agent, then transforming them when agents coordinate. That lowers drift after movement because a local record needs only the agent pose to stay useful.

heat.caption: Darker means the team is more likely to act on stale or conflicting state.

reads.html: This is a measure of how likely the agents are to agree on what the world currently looks like.
The system tracks objects in agent-centered coordinates and transforms them into a shared scene so the next joint action is based on a more consistent state record.

paras: The memory design helps because local coordinates are stable under motion. If an object is stored as two steps in front of agent A, then after A moves you can update that relation with a simple pose transform instead of rebuilding the whole scene from scratch. That cuts stale object records, so fewer actions are aimed at the wrong place.

The joint solver helps because it chooses actions for the whole team at once. Independent choices often fail when two actions depend on the same door, path, or object. Mosaic avoids that by enforcing feasibility and ordering inside the selection step, so the system spends fewer turns recovering from avoidable conflicts.

stages.s: Store objects in each agent's local frame
Transform into a shared scene when coordination is needed
Solve one feasible action set for the team
Fewer failed actions and shorter task completion time

math.words: At each step, pick the action set that gives the largest total task gain while obeying feasibility and coordination constraints.
math.equation: choose a* = argmax_a sum_i score(i, a_i) subject to feasible(a) = 1
symbols: the action assigned to agent i at the current step
the value of giving action a_i to agent i, based on task progress
a check that the whole action set respects reachability, ordering, and conflict rules

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Two agents need a mug from a closed cabinet.
Agent A can open the cabinet now.
Agent B can pick the mug only after the cabinet is open.
Independent choice may give A=pick and B=pick, which fails for both.
The solver checks feasibility and instead picks A=open, B=wait.
On the next step it picks A=move away, B=pick.
The team finishes in two valid steps because the solver enforced the right order.

math.note: The paper uses integer linear programming to solve this selection problem exactly under step-level constraints.

items.html: If an agent misreads the scene, then the transformed shared view is also wrong because the system starts from that local record.
If the solver does not encode an important physical rule, then it may approve an action set that still fails in the environment because the rule was never checked.

items.b: Solver cost at very large scale.
items.html: As the number of agents and candidate actions grows, solving the joint step can take longer because the search space gets larger.
The method pays off when failed actions are a major source of delay, because better state tracking and compatibility checks remove exactly that waste.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small grid world with two agents, a door, and two objects. Give each agent only a local view. Compare two systems: one with plain shared text memory and independent action choice, and one with local-coordinate memory plus a joint constraint solver. Measure completion time, failed actions, and repeated planning calls. The demo should show that the second system finishes faster because it keeps a cleaner world record and prevents incompatible actions before they are executed.
demo.metric_eq: failure_rate = failed_actions / attempted_actions ; time_gain = (baseline_time - mosaic_time) / baseline_time
demo.closing: The demo must show fewer failed actions and shorter completion time for the same tasks.
